He is mentioned {{in|FO4}} and {{in|FO76|noin}}. {{FOTV appearances |9=201 |11=203 |13=205 |14=206 |15=207 |16=208 }} ==Behind the scenes== ===''Fallout: New Vegas''=== [[File:Rene Auberjonois booth.png|thumb|220px|right|Mr. House's voice actor, [[René Auberjonois]], in the voiceover booth]] * In ''Fallout: New Vegas'', House is voiced by actor [[René Auberjonois]] (1940–2019), also known for his role as [[w:c:memory-alpha:Odo|Odo]] on ''[[w:c:memory-alpha:Star Trek: Deep Space Nine|Star Trek: Deep Space Nine]]'' and sharing the screen with [[Michael Dorn]] and [[William Sadler]] who voice [[Marcus]] and [[Victor (Securitron)|Victor]], respectively. ** Senior producer [[Jason Bergman]] had Auberjonois as his first and only choice for the role of Mr. House during the game's casting process; Bergman described himself as "gung ho about Rene from day one."[https://web.archive.org/web/20200218164147/http://forums.bethsoft.com/topic/1223886-wheres-wal-jason-bergman-thread-2/page-2 Jason Bergman on the Bethesda Forums (archived)]: ''"He was my first choice, that's for sure. And my only choice, actually. For some other roles we had actors we tried to get, but more often than not we got our first choice. I don't even remember who else was suggested for House, since I was so gung ho about Rene from day one."'' ** In localized versions of the game, his voice is dubbed by Frédéric Cerdal (French, also the dubbed voice of [[Victor (Securitron)|Victor]]), Masashi Hirose (Japanese) and Roberto Encinas (Spanish, also the dubbed voice of [[Raul Tejada]]). * Mr. House is the King of Diamonds in the deck of [[Vault playing cards]] included with the ''[[Fallout: New Vegas#Collector's Edition|Collector's Edition]]'' of ''Fallout: New Vegas''. * The challenge [[A Slave Obeys]] requires the player character to kill Mr. House with the [[9 iron]] or [[Driver Nephi]]'s [[Nephi's golf driver|golf club]]. This is a reference to the video game ''[[Wikipedia:BioShock|BioShock]]'', where the player beats the antagonist Andrew Ryan to death with a 9 iron while he repeats the words "A man chooses, a slave obeys." Both characters were based in part on Howard Hughes and share other traits. * In casino parlance, "the house" refers generally to the gambler's opponent, the casino itself, as in the idiom "[[The House Always Wins|the house always wins]]." ====Developer quotes==== {{Quotation|[Question: ''The Realpolitik analyses of the NCR and the Legion were outlined quite well by Marcus in New Vegas. But what are your ultimate thoughts on House?'']
He's a laissez-faire dictator. "Do whatever you want as long as you don't cross me." Mr. House doesn't care about other people and what they do as long as Vegas remains prosperous and he remains in control.|[[Joshua Sawyer]]'s [[Joshua Sawyer Formspring posts/2011|Formspring on Robert House's ideology]]}} {{Quotation|[Question: ''Perhaps Mr. House is 'dictatorial' to the extent that he won't permit anyone to breach his quasi-governmental monopoly on force, but otherwise I'm not sure what you mean by 'laissez-faire dictator,' which seems like one heck of an oxymoron.'']
He doesn't place many restrictions on people -- or on businesses -- but he always gets his cut, and when he does make a decree, it's absolute. New Vegas is a place where people have to feel like they can do whatever they want. Mr. House doesn't restrict sexual behavior, drug use, or most other types of personal behavior. The only people who really feel his direct presence are representatives of other governments, those who explicitly cross him, and the heads of the families who have to give him a share of his profits.|[[Joshua Sawyer]]'s [[Joshua Sawyer Formspring posts/2011|Formspring on Robert House's ideology]]}} {{Quotation|[Question: ''How would you describe Mr. House's Ideology? I know that he's rather authoritarian when it comes to political freedoms, but what about on economic issues? He was my favorite character in the game, and whoever wrote him did an outstanding job.'']
He's also authoritarian on economic issues within certain boundaries. In the same way that a fascist government would exert authority on the various production/capital resources involved in a market, Mr. House exerts his authority on The Strip's operation. Ultimately, he wants The Strip to be (extremely) profitable and to retain independence from NCR/CL. However, he does not want the families to be independent from his authority, so he does what he can to keep them under his thumb. He doesn't want to micromanage what they do, but he also knows that allowing them to do whatever they want could eventually lead to the downfall of his authority or fighting between the families (which would also undermine his authority).
Really, the main area in which Mr. House is "liberal" is in personal consumption and behavior. As long as it makes him money and doesn't create instability or feuding on The Strip, he allows it.|[[Joshua Sawyer]]'s [[Joshua Sawyer Formspring posts/2012|Formspring on Robert House's ideology]]}} ====Developer context==== * Mr. House was created and written by [[John Gonzalez]].[https://web.archive.org/web/20221217180022/https://twitter.com/jesawyer/status/1604171903978962944 Joshua Sawyer on Twitter]: ''"He created and wrote House, designed the families of The Strip, and wrote many major characters, including House, Caesar, Benny, Yes Man, and Vulpes Inculta. He also wrote Ricky and Stella in Honest Hearts as well as all of the Survivalist/Randall Clark logs. 3/8"''Question: ''"Was Ayn Rand by any chance part of the inspiration for Mr. House? He seems very much like her type of heroic businessman and laissez-faire capitalist."''
[[Joshua Sawyer]]: ''"He was most heavily inspired by Howard Hughes. John Gonzalez created and wrote all of Mr. House's dialogue, so he might be able to offer more detailed insight."''

We intentionally left the Courier's origins and the exact nature of the initial transaction vague." ====Historical and political context==== * Robert House is based on [[wikipedia:Howard Hughes|Howard Hughes]], who was similarly a reclusive millionaire with ties to the real world [[wikipedia:Las Vegas Strip|Las Vegas Strip]]. Hughes had a habit of raising his left eyebrow in photographs, which shows on House's monitor portrait. The [[House Resort]] contains a large portrait of Mr. House standing in front of an enormous, bipedal robot; the portrait is based on a real-world photograph of Howard Hughes standing in front of a Boeing 100A aircraft in 1934.[https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/49/Howard_Hughes.jpg Hughes Boeing 100A photo] ** Jane, House's Securitron companion, is a reference to real world actress [[Wikipedia:Jane Russell|Jane Russell]], who worked for Hughes' production company for several years. ** Like Hughes, House used a body double for his public facing persona before the Great War. * When asked about House's political ideology, [[Chris Avellone]] deferred a more definitive answer to [[John Gonzalez]], as he was the main writer for House. However, Avellone did say that while he "wasn't aware of any [particular] ideology, [the developers] didn't usually lean on any specific real world ideologies when crafting characters - although [people] have interpreted them as such."[https://archive.is/IyVnp Chris Avellone on Twitter]: ''"John Gonzalez (lead writer) might be the best one to ask, as he wrote him. While I wasn't aware of any particlar{{sic}} ideology, we didn't usually lean on any specific real world ideologies when crafting characters - although ppl have interpreted them as such."'' However, in the "[[Behind the Bright Lights & Big City]]" section of the collector's edition ''[[Fallout: New Vegas Official Game Guide]]'', House is described as a "libertarian dictator."''"So long as Mr. House's basic rules are followed, his intentions are to take a "hands off" approach towards the subjects of his kingdom; he is effectively a libertarian dictator creating his own version of paradise rooted in the old world. If the player supports Mr. House, she is supporting the New Vegas libertopia, a place where the strong rule unfettered for as long as they stay strong and where the weak are continually trampled underfoot. But it's a place where Mr. House wants you to dream, that someday, you could be on of the strong."''
([[Behind the Bright Lights & Big City]], ''[[Fallout: New Vegas Official Game Guide]]'' collector's edition, p. 463 ====Cut content==== {{FNVCC}} * Mr. House's computer screen originally had a different portrait displayed on it, featuring more of his body, facing slightly off-center, and with a somewhat different face (see [[#Gallery|below]]). In this dialogue, House would have stated that he will not attack the player character if they simply walk away. {{FNVCC|end}} ===''Fallout'' TV series=== * {{Note|(Note 2)}} In the ''Fallout'' TV series, Robert House is played by actor [[Justin Theroux]], starting from the show's second season. This was explicitly confirmed in promotional materials and interviews for the show around the time of season 2's release.[https://archive.ph/eRVrF Gizmodo: "In 'Fallout' Season 2's First Trailer, All Roads Lead to New Vegas" (archived)] Meanwhile, [[Rafi Silver]] plays Mr. House's body double, who first appeared in the season 1 finale "[[The Beginning]]." However, within the show itself, Silver's character was credited as Robert House both in "The Beginning" and in the first episode of season 2, "[[The Innovator]];" he was first credited as the Robert House double in "[[The Wrangler]]." Theroux's character remains unnamed in the credits of all of the season 2 episodes he appears in, though the show itself confirms he is the actual Robert House. ** In an interview from December 2025, Geneva Robertson-Dworet and Justin Theroux alluded to the relationship between Theroux's House and Silver's House body double. Robertson-Dworet commented that this was based on Howard Hughes' increasing reclusiveness near the end of his life, stating that the writers wanted to depict House as someone "constantly playing tricks on the world" and "maybe somewhat scared to go out because, think of what a targeted man he is." Theroux suggested that House could have "become so paranoid, or so rarefied, that he needs to live above Las Vegas in a very protected place," also noting that the setting of the late 2070s made it "still possible to have avatars in the world where people wouldn't recognize [House]." * Prior to the release of season 2, Theroux's appearance as House was spotlighted in a ''GQ'' article. According to [[Geneva Robertson-Dworet]] and [[Jonathan Nolan]], the showrunners behind the TV series were interested in exploring House as a character, especially prior to the Great War. This interest was due to House himself being synonymous with Vegas, and they had already decided on going there as the primary setting of season 2. Additionally, they saw House's character as being relevant in the real world in 2025, at a time when "very wealthy technocrats have undue influence in the world," according to Nolan.[https://archive.ph/ZG0ma GQ: "First Look at Justin Theroux in ''Fallout'' Season 2: Inside the Show's Big Trip to Vegas" (archived)] ** Theroux was convinced to join the cast of ''Fallout''{{'}}s second season by [[Walton Goggins]], who is a close friend of Theroux. Theroux was already admired as an actor by Jonathan Nolan, who suggested to Goggins that he make the pitch. Prior to the offer, Theroux had neither seen the ''Fallout'' show nor played a ''Fallout'' game, but he accepted the offer and studied House's character by watching gameplay videos of ''Fallout: New Vegas'' on YouTube. According to Theroux, he believed Nolan saw real-world parallels in the present to the type of character House was, while Theroux himself personally interpreted House's character as being similar to [[wikipedia:Robert McNamara|Robert McNamara]], the real-world Secretary of Defense under [[wikipedia:John F. Kennedy|John F. Kennedy]] and [[wikipedia:Lyndon B. Johnson|Lyndon B. Johnson]], especially in relation to his prediction of nuclear threat at the height of the [[Cold War]]. Theroux also mentioned Howard Hughes as a reference point for his performance, reflecting how Hughes was cited as a significant influence for House's character as played by [[René Auberjonois]] during the original development of ''Fallout: New Vegas''. ** As other inspirations, Theroux also cited studying "radio announcers, newsmen and people who had [House's] specific dialect."[https://archive.ph/g9WiA Screen Rant: "Fallout Season 2: Justin Theroux On Taking Over Iconic Mr. House Role" (archived)] * After the release of "The Handoff," [[Geneva Robertson-Dworet]] said in an interview that a representation of Robert House powered by cold fusion seemed like the "ultimate version" of House. She explained that the writers viewed this as something it made sense for House, as a person interested in robotics and self-preservation, to develop, and that it also allowed the writers to include House in the story without overruling players' gameplay experiences in ''Fallout: New Vegas''. However, she declined to state whether this would be the "''final'' final form" of House in the series. * In a GQ interview following the release of "The Strip," Walton Goggins was asked how the scene between the Ghoul and Robert House's avatar in the Lucky 38 penthouse during "The Strip" was filmed. Goggins revealed that both he and Justin Theroux were fitted with 35mm camera rigs, with Theroux being projected in full costume onto the screen in real-time so both actors could play off of each other and convey their characters' relationship; Goggins agreed with the interviewer's comparison of the situation to a Zoom call.[https://www.gq.com/story/walton-goggins-fallout-season-2-finale-interview 'Fallout' Star Walton Goggins Says the Season 2 Finale Was All About 'Hope' | GQ: (February 5, 2026)] ==Bugs== *{{Platforms|pc,ps3,xbox360}} A Medicine 35 check can be repeatedly accessed in Mr. House's dialogue, gaining XP each time.{{Verify|verified}} *{{Platforms|pc}} Activating Mr. House fails to start dialogue, rendering him useless (the mainframe). '''Julia Masters''' was a member of the pre-[[Great War|War]] [[REPCONN Aerospace]] [[Pre-War companies|company]], serving as its chief financial officer (CFO). She is [[Fallout: New Vegas characters|mentioned]] {{In|FNV}} and appears {{In|FOTV}}.

==Background==
===Meeting with Vault-Tec===
At some point prior to the [[Great War]], Julia was invited to attend a meeting at the Southern California [[Vault-Tec headquarters (TV series)|headquarters]] of the [[Vault-Tec Corporation]] in [[Los Angeles]], along with Vault-Tec's [[Barb Howard]] and [[Bud Askins]], [[Big MT (company)|Big MT]]'s [[Frederick Sinclair]], [[West Tek]]'s [[Leon Von Felden]] and [[RobCo Industries]]'s [[Robert House]]. She was informed of Vault-Tec's protracted plans to extend their network of [[Vault]]s across the nation and heard their offer of selecting some vaults to be used for [[Vault#True purpose|social experiments]] at the behest of the corporate heads; Masters herself mentioned REPCONN had been developing an intelligent robot that "brings milk to the front door," and that she would like to see a Vault governed by it.<ref>[[Fallout (TV series)|''Fallout'']] Season 1 Episode 8, "[[The Beginning]]"</ref>

===Corporate espionage===
When [[Poseidon Energy]] sought to buy out REPCONN, she and [[Leonard Steeple|Vice President Leonard Steeple]] worked together to keep REPCONN independent, successfully stopping the Poseidon deal from occurring. However, when [[RobCo Industries]] later made an offer to buy the company, Julia instead worked with [[Piers Isley|General Manager Piers Isley]] to push the deal through to completion while Steeple was out of commission because of an illness.<ref name="julia">[[REPCONN headquarters terminal entries#Inter-office_Correspondence_.233262173|REPCONN headquarters terminal entries; terminal, Inter-office Correspondence #3262173]]</ref> On Leonard's return, he heard about the deal and attempted to stop the buyout, hoping to enlist Julia's support, which Julia pretended to agree with. In reality, she used Leonard's message to confirm his standing before convincing the REPCONN board to hold a vote of no confidence against Leonard, removing him from his position and freeing up the way for the RobCo deal.<ref>[[REPCONN headquarters terminal entries#Inter-office_Correspondence_.233262178|REPCONN headquarters terminal entries; terminal, Inter-office Correspondence #3262178]]</ref><ref>[[REPCONN headquarters terminal entries#Inter-office_Correspondence_.233262179|REPCONN headquarters terminal entries; terminal, Inter-office Correspondence #3262179]]</ref> Julia then took over Leonard's duties interim until the RobCo merger took place and [[Carl Rook]] became REPCONN's vice president.<ref>[[REPCONN headquarters terminal entries#Inter-office_Correspondence_.233262725|REPCONN headquarters terminal entries; terminal, Inter-office Correspondence #3262725]]</ref>

Following the merger, however, Julia proved to be no more loyal to RobCo than to REPCONN before it. She began stealing trade secrets from REPCONN to sell to an unknown outside party, including trade information related to the Quantum Plasma Modulation Matter Injection Rifle project, as well as the password to Piers Isley's computer, and conspired to have her contacts steal the project's [[Q-35 matter modulator|Q-35 model prototype]] while it was in transit to the [[Department of Defense]].<ref>[[REPCONN headquarters terminal entries#Encrypted Message|REPCONN headquarters terminal entries; terminal, Encrypted Message]]</ref>

[[Sara Wang]], an IT specialist for REPCONN, had detected the encrypted messages sent by Julia, but did not know she was the one sending them. Sara believed that Julia's recipient was Poseidon Energy, but she did not have enough evidence to back her claim.<ref>[[REPCONN headquarters terminal entries#Inter-office_Correspondence_.233457785|REPCONN headquarters terminal entries; terminal, Inter-office Correspondence #3457785]]</ref> Ulimately, like the rest of America, Julia's plans went up in fire at the breakout of the Great War.

==Appearances==
Julia Masters is mentioned {{In|FNV}} and appears in the [[Fallout (TV series)|''Fallout'' TV series]], where she is portrayed by [[Rebecca Watson]].

They'll be Stone Age creatures, probably eat whoever steps out of your Vaults.}} '''Leon Von Felden''' was a pre-[[Great War|War]] scientist and employee of [[West Tek]] who headed the [[Forced Evolutionary Virus]] Project at the [[The Glow|West Tek Research Facility]] and later the [[Mariposa Military Base]], where he possessed the highest corporate security clearance.[[West Tek records]] He is mentioned {{In|FO1}} and {{In|FO3|noin}} and appears {{In|FOTV}}. ==Background== ===Meeting with Vault-Tec=== At some point prior to the [[Great War]], Leon was invited to attend a meeting at the Southern California [[Vault-Tec headquarters (TV series)|headquarters]] of the [[Vault-Tec Corporation]] in [[Los Angeles]], along with Vault-Tec executives [[Barb Howard]] and [[Bud Askins]], [[Big MT (company)|Big MT]] representative [[Frederick Sinclair]], [[REPCONN Aerospace]] CFO [[Julia Masters]] and [[RobCo Industries]] CEO [[Robert House]]. He was informed of Vault-Tec's protracted plans to extend their network of [[Vault]]s across the nation and heard their offer of selecting some vaults to be used for [[Vault#True purpose|social experiments]] at the behest of the corporate heads; while he was skeptical of the Vaults' creation, Von Felden posited a scenario for a Vault developing super mutant soldiers using "illegal immigrants."[[Frederick Sinclair]]: ''"We could intentionally overcrowd a vault so people have to compete to survive inside it."''
[[Julia Masters]]: ''"We have been developing a robot that delivers milk to the front door. It's quite intelligent. I would like to see a vault governed by it."''
Leon Von Felden: ''"What about using a vault to develop a super-mutant soldier using illegal immigrants?"''
({{FOTV|1|8}}) ===The Mariposa Rebellion=== Later in October 2077, when the [[Brotherhood of Steel#The Mariposa Rebellion|Mariposa Rebellion]] took place, Von Felden was one of the last scientists to be interrogated after the base's [[United States Armed Forces|military]] detachment discovered the FEV experiments going on there. He was being interrogated on [[Timeline (2050-2099)#2077|October 23]] when Mariposa lost contact with the outside world halfway through.[[Captain Maxson's diary#Oct. 23 2077|Captain Maxson's diary]]: ''"Oct. 23 2077''
''I can't believe those bastards finally did it. Damn them all to Hell. They finally let the A-Bombs fly. We were right in the middle of trying to pry the real story out of von Felden when we completely lost contact. I have a feeling the research center was hit hard. I don't know why, just call it a gut feeling. It seems inconceivable that we were not targeted. I'm sure China will make up for that oversight real soon. Luckily, we had moved our families from outside into the facility the day before yesterday. We do not yet know if the fallout has reached this area."'' Without any expectation of bringing the scientist to justice for his crimes, Captain [[Roger Maxson]] ordered Von Felden's summary execution. He also arranged for all the scientists to receive a proper burial, if only to ease his own conscience.[[Captain Maxson's diary#Oct. 26 2077|Captain Maxson's diary]]: ''"Oct. 26 2077''
''I convinced the men that we should bury the scientists. I don't know why...perhaps it was to ease my conscience. I finally started to believe their stories when the last one was dying.''
